title: The dart of grief
hookLine: life is short and uncertain; draw out the dart of lamentation

cards: There's a drawer in many homes that nobody opens much. A watch that stopped. A card in a handwriting you'd know anywhere.

A phone number you can't quite bring yourself to delete. Grief has a way of lodging somewhere and staying. The Salla Sutta, the discourse on the dart, eighth in the Sutta Nipata's third chapter, doesn't open with comfort.
It opens with the plain facts of death, and then a picture every archer and every healer in ancient India would have known: something sharp, stuck in the chest, that has to come out.

teach.b: The verses begin bluntly. The life of mortals is unmarked by any sign of how long it will last, short, and tied up with pain. There's no way for those born not to die.

As ripe fruit is in danger of falling early, so the born are always in danger of death. As clay pots made by a potter all end up broken, so it is with life. Young and old, foolish and wise, all go under death's power.
Even as relatives look on, weeping, each one is led away. Then the turn. The wise, seeing how the world is, don't add grief on grief.
Weeping and wailing, the poem says, don't bring back the one who's gone; they only harm the one who weeps, who grows thin and pale, while the dead are not helped at all.

teach.h: THE DART IS IN THE MOURNER.
teach.b: So draw out the dart: the dart of lamenting, of longing, of grief, and you'll find peace. Two things are worth noticing.
First, the dart is in the mourner, not in the one who died. The poem isn't saying the loss doesn't matter. It's saying the wound is real and can heal.
Second, Pali salla is a barbed arrow or a splinter, the thing a healer pulls out. The poem is firm: lamenting helps no one. But its picture is a healer's, not a judge's.
A barb is drawn out with care, not something you're blamed for carrying.

how: Verses on impermanence are often chanted at Buddhist funerals and memorial services, and in many Theravada communities monks are invited to chant and teach for the family in the days after a death.

o: a barbed dart, lodged and needing care to remove
a mourning song sung at a funeral
a burial ground where the dead are laid

games.q: the dart of grief: tap the pairs.
p: made by a potter, all end broken
don't bring back the one gone

s: the Salla Sutta says the dead are helped by long mourning
it says weeping harms the mourner and doesn't help the one who has died.
the poem compares mortals to clay pots made by a potter
as the potter's pots all end up broken, so it is with life.
in the image, the dart is lodged in the one who grieves
the wound is in the mourner, and the poem asks that it be drawn out.

games.q: someone you love has died. you've wept for days and can't eat. according to the Salla Sutta, what helps the one who has died?
o: more weeping, to show how much they mattered.
nothing in your weeping helps them; it only harms you.
games.why: the poem says plainly that lamenting doesn't reach the dead and only wears down the living. so it asks the mourner to draw out the dart.

practice: If there's someone you've lost, a person, an animal, a time of your life, let them come to mind, and find where the feeling sits: the chest, the throat, behind the eyes.
Breathe near it, the way you'd sit beside someone in a hospital bed. If nothing comes, think of someone who is grieving, and simply wish them ease.

wordCard.voice: Salla, a barbed dart. In the Salla Sutta, lamenting lodged in the one who mourns, a real wound, which can be drawn out.

orig.note: Pali salla: a dart, barbed arrow or splinter. the Salla Sutta is Sn 3.8.

carryVoice: Your line: draw out the dart. Gently, the way a healer would. Rest well, and see you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sutta Nipata 3.8 (Salla Sutta), the dart of grief
